Thank you for submitting your article "Conjunction of Factors Triggering Waves of Seasonal Influenza" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by one of the original peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Prabhat Jha as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission. We appreciate your revisions to the organization of the text and interpretation of the results, and think that many of the changes improve the readability and flow of the paper and clarify the goals of the analysis. Nevertheless, we still have remaining concerns about some parts of the analyses and about the sparsity of information for others. Hence we think that the article is still not ready to be published in its current state.

We would like to avoid multiple further rounds of revision, so we can give you one more opportunity to address the remaining issues before a final decision about the manuscript is made.

The remaining issues with the manuscript can be divided into two categories: (i) substantial scientific issues that need to be addressed before the manuscript is published, (ii) recommendations about the description of the work that we strongly encourage you to take but which are optional.

Essential revisions about scientific content:i) (Discussion, second paragraph) It is still difficult to interpret the results related to short-range and long-range travel. We were unable to find the regression results for the full set of data weeks in the supplement. Also, there is not enough detail in the analysis description to see how Figure 5 Plates C-F demonstrate that local connections are more explanatory than airport connections.

ii) The highlighted areas (greater incidence) in the first flu season snapshot for Figures 3A-H each should match relatively well to the maps in Figure 7B (or at least some unspecified subset of "high incidence treatment counties"). While the county-matching results to point to initiation at coasts, 2006-2007 in Figure 3 seems to initiate from the West Coast and 2010 in Figure 7 has a scattered pattern across the middle of the US. Please check this or justify the differences.

iii) Also related to Figure 7, was there also a geographic constraint on the choice of the matched control counties? It is surprising that everything is so geographically clustered.

Recommendations about presentation of content:

i) It would be useful to provide a quantitative example of how to interpret one of the results in Figure 2A.

ii) (Subsection “The weather/humidity paradox”) This humidity paradox has come up quite a bit recently and it may be cleaner to have a fuller treatment of this in the Discussion.

iii) The subsection on Variable and model selection at the end of the Discussion seems out of place. Was this meant to be moved to the Materials and methods?

iv) Please point out the Discussion section describing the generalizability of the findings (as mentioned in the response).

v) The Conclusion section does much more of the storytelling that would be expected from a Discussion. It may be more compelling to kick off the Discussion with the analogy describing the epidemiological findings, and then elaborate on the strengths of using multiple methods to corroborate statistical findings.

vi) You may consider condensing the figures in the main text to those that present primary findings (removing some plates and potentially reducing the total number of figures). The figures are all visually appealing, but every single one is densely packed with primary findings, descriptive information, data processing details, and diagnostics/sensitivity. Some of the main takeaways may get lost.

vii) Figure 2 might be more aptly named "Putative determinants of seasonal influenza onset[…]"

viii) Figure 4, Plate I: Please add an explanation of the red circles to the legend title or caption.

ix) Please provide some explanation of how you developed the 126 models examined in Approach 2. Based on the models listed in Table 5 and in the supplement, it seems that there is substantial variation in the number of predictors included in the model and all of the models appear to include multiple autoregressive terms for the same environmental and travel predictors. What is the motivation for this approach? In addition, it would be good to better understand the random effects in the model (subsection “Approach 2: Poisson Regression on Putative Factors”, first paragraph) and the motivation for this model structure. Does this term include a spatial smoothing component?

results.result: The study utilized a large-scale insurance claims database (Truven MarketScan) covering 150 million individuals over 9 years (2003-2012), processing 4.6 billion service claims and identifying nearly 6 billion diagnosis codes to track influenza-like illnesses.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C23, and C24 collectively establish the data source and scale. The explicit description of database size, temporal coverage, and volume of processed claims provides clear documentation of the study's data foundation. The scale is unprecedented for this type of analysis.

results.result: Seasonal influenza epidemics in the US consistently initiate in the South/Southeastern regions and propagate northward, originating in areas with high mean maximum specific humidity, high average temperature, and low average air pressure, particularly near coastal regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C60, and C10 converge on the geographic pattern of epidemic initiation. The south-to-north propagation is demonstrated through multiple data visualizations (Figure 2A-H, movie) and cannot be explained by population density alone (C60). Weather conditions in southern coastal areas (C10) provide mechanistic context for this pattern.

results.result: Drops in specific humidity (up to 4 weeks prior) and average temperature (1-3 weeks prior) significantly influence epidemic spread, especially when temperature drops are accompanied by decreases in specific humidity, wind speed, and solar flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C12 describe temporal weather dynamics preceding epidemics. The specific time windows and combinations of meteorological factors are explicitly stated with reference to regression analysis results. C12 cites experimental support (Lowen et al., 2008), strengthening the claim.

results.result: Antigenic diversity in viral proteins shows differential effects on epidemic triggering: HA, NA, and M1 diversity inhibits triggering while M2 diversity enhances it. Antigenic diversity is strongly correlated with vaccination coverage, reflecting theoretical predictions about evolutionary pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C32, and C33 establish the role of viral evolution. The opposite directional effects of different proteins (C13) are explicitly stated from regression results. The strong dependence between antigenic diversity and vaccination (C32, C33) is shown in Figure 1J-M with theoretical support from Boni et al. (2006).

results.result: Short-range land travel is significantly more important than long-range air travel for sustaining epidemic propagation, though airport proximity is important for initial epidemic triggering. Land connectivity effects are an order of magnitude stronger than air travel effects during epidemic spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 and C91-C93 converge from three analytical approaches. Granger causality analysis (C21), mixed-effect regression (C22), and all-weeks analysis (C20) consistently show stronger local effects. The distinction between triggering (where airports matter, C19, C91) versus propagation (where land travel dominates, C18, C93) is well-supported across methods.

results.result: Autocorrelation of influenza infection rates 1-2 weeks prior to epidemic onset in source counties is predictive of epidemic wave origin.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 describes a temporal autocorrelation effect explicitly identified in the regression analysis. This represents the self-reinforcing nature of local outbreaks and is a standard epidemiological pattern.

results.result: The US Southern region, particularly the East/South/Central census region (MS, AL, TN, KY), exhibits unusually high social connectivity compared to the national average, with more close friends, more neighbor friendships, and more frequent social visits.
results.evaluation: Claims C17 and C61-C64 present social connectivity data from GSS surveys shown in Table 1. The specific numerical comparisons (e.g., 12.76 vs 7.57 close friends) provide quantitative support. This social connectivity may contribute to epidemic dynamics in these regions.

results.result: Vaccination coverage is not a significant predictor of influenza onset/triggering period in the regression models.
results.evaluation: Claim C9 states vaccination coverage failed to reach significance, but the manuscript also notes (C32) that vaccination strongly affects antigenic diversity, and vaccination variables are included in the best model despite not being individually significant. The lack of significance may reflect collinearity with antigenic diversity rather than true lack of effect. The interpretation is ambiguous.

results.result: The best regression model demonstrates predictive capability with AUC values of approximately 80% (ranging 0.74-0.87) on out-of-sample data from three seasons (2009-2011), correctly identifying South/Southeastern counties as trigger zones.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C77-C80, C88, and C100 establish predictive validation. ROC analysis (C77) on held-out data shows consistent AUC around 80% (C3, C78). Geographic predictions match expected trigger zones (C79), and correlation with observed data is significant (C80). Cross-validation justifies the model selection approach (C100).

results.result: The study employed three orthogonal analytical approaches (non-parametric Granger analysis, mixed-effect Poisson regression, and county-matching analysis) to systematically compare numerous putative epidemic triggers in an integrative framework, with convergent conclusions strengthening causal inference.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C86-C87, C89-C90 describe the methodological innovation. The use of three different statistical approaches (C31, C86) to test the same hypotheses (C87) in an integrative study (C89) is explicitly stated. Convergence across methods (C90) reduces likelihood of artifacts. This represents a novel methodological contribution.

results.result: County-matching analysis (Approach 3) identified statistically significant combinations of weather factors predicting epidemic onset, with specific humidity and average temperature (and their temporal variations) being the most consistently important factors across seasons.

The p-values and odds ratios (C65-C71) demonstrate statistical significance for various factor combinations. results.result: The study employed detailed operational definitions for key variables including county neighborhoods (50-mile threshold), trigger periods (5-6 weeks), dispersion metrics (largest connected component), vaccination coverage (20-week cumulative), and utilized multiple high-resolution data sources for weather, travel, and viral sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C52 document methodological details and data sources. These operational definitions are clearly stated and appropriately cited. The explicit documentation of thresholds, time windows, and data sources supports reproducibility, though some choices (e.g., 50-mile threshold, 20-week vaccination window) appear somewhat arbitrary.

results.result: The Truven insurance claims data correlates well with CDC ILI data (ρ=0.91, p=3.5×10^-201) though the relationship is non-linear, and causality coefficients from Granger analysis have similar interpretations to regression coefficients.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C57, and C58 establish data validity and methodological consistency. The strong correlation with CDC data (C57) validates the insurance claims approach. The non-linearity is attributed to CDC data resolution. Consistency between Granger and regression coefficients (C58) supports convergent validity across methods.

results.result: Model selection compared 126 different regression models using DIC, with the best model achieving DIC=185,926.6. While DIC has known limitations (tendency to select overfits) and a greedy search approach was used, coefficient directions remained stable across models and model informativeness increased with complexity.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 and C98-C99 describe model selection. The extensive comparison (126 models, C73) and stability of coefficient signs (C74-C75) support robustness. However, the authors acknowledge DIC limitations (C98) and non-optimal search (C99), which are appropriate caveats. The cross-validation results (referenced in C100) partially mitigate these concerns.

results.result: The three analytical approaches have complementary strengths and limitations: Approach 2 (regression) is powerful for detecting interactions but susceptible to bias in unbalanced data; Approach 3 (matching) balances observational data but loses statistical power with complex treatments; Approach 1 (Granger) is non-parametric but focuses only on directional flows.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 explicitly describe methodological trade-offs. The authors transparently acknowledge that each approach has distinct strengths (C101, C103, C104) and limitations (C102, C105). This honest assessment of methodological constraints strengthens confidence in the convergent findings.

results.result: Prior studies have reached conflicting conclusions about humidity's role in influenza: one US study (1973-2002) identified absolute humidity as especially critical for mortality, while a Netherlands study attributed only 3% of variation to humidity (vs. 57% to host depletion), and school holidays showed no significant effect in the Netherlands study.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 accurately cite prior literature (Barreca & Shimshack 2012; te Beest et al. 2013; Shaman & Kohn 2009). These citations establish the context of conflicting prior findings that motivated the current integrative study. The citations appear accurate based on the descriptions provided.

results.result: The methods and analytical tools developed should be broadly applicable to other pathogens and geographic regions due to universal virus/host biology, though specific conclusions about US influenza patterns may not generalize. The approach has potential applications beyond epidemiology to other spatio-temporal dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 make assertions about generalizability. While the methods are indeed general (C95, C97), the claims about universal applicability (C94) are speculative. The authors appropriately hedge (C96) that specific findings may not generalize. However, no empirical validation in other contexts is provided, making these claims about future applicability uncertain.
